holidays.name: National Corn Chip Day
holidays.description: A crunchy salute to the humble fried cornmeal snack. It is the perfect excuse to dunk, scoop, and pile on the nachos, and to crunch loudly without apology.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial snack observance of unclear origin. It celebrates the corn chip, which became a popular American snack in the 1930s.
holidays.funFact: The corn chip is most closely linked to Elmer Doolin. In the 1930s he bought a corn chip recipe and business in San Antonio, Texas, and that business grew into the Fritos brand.

holidays.name: National Puzzle Day
holidays.description: A day for jigsaws, crosswords, sudoku, riddles, and brain teasers. Challenge your mind, stump your friends, and finally finish the 1,000-piece puzzle that has been sitting on the dining table.
holidays.origin: National Puzzle Day was created by puzzle author and writer Jodi Jill. It has been observed in the United States on January 29 since the early 1990s.
holidays.funFact: The first jigsaw puzzle is credited to London mapmaker John Spilsbury, who around 1760 mounted a map on wood and cut it into pieces to teach geography.

holidays.name: Freethinkers Day (Thomas Paine Day)
holidays.description: A celebration of skeptics, questioners, and independent thinkers. It honors reason over dogma and the willingness to ask awkward questions at dinner parties.
holidays.origin: The day marks the birthday of Thomas Paine, born January 29, 1737. He wrote the pamphlet Common Sense, which helped fuel the American Revolution, and later wrote The Age of Reason.
holidays.funFact: Common Sense was published in 1776 and sold an estimated 100,000 or more copies in a few months. That was a huge number for the small colonial population of the time.
